newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire says it launched new air raids on east.
newsitem.headline: Zaire says it launched new air raids on east.

text.p: Zaire announced new bombing raids on rebel-held towns in the east on Tuesday as African foreign ministers arrived in the capital for talks on bringing peace to Central Africa's volatile Great Lakes region.
A defence ministry official in Kinshasa said government planes bombed Bukavu, Shabunda and Walikale on Tuesday morning, but no independent confirmation of the new raids was available.
Aid workers in Bukavu reported shortly after nightfall that there had been no raids on the city on Tuesday.

In Geneva, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, appealed for a halt to the bombing and expressed concern about the plight of refugees at Tingi Tingi camp where the world body says Rwandan Hutu hardliners are arming.
Relief workers in the east said thousands of panic-stricken civilians had fled their homes following Monday's government air raids which killed at least 19 people.

"There is a continuous flow of movement from Bukavu. It does not exceed perhaps 20 percent of the population but it is in the thousands," said Marcel van Soest of the charity, Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF) in the eastern rebel headquarters city of Goma.
"People in panic are fleeing in all directions," an aid worker in the Bukavu area said.
Aid workers keeping track of bodies pulled from rubble put the latest death toll at 19. Earlier reports spoke of 21 dead.
The air raids represent a change in tack in the faltering government counter-offensive launched on January 20 to retake territory from rebels who took up arms in October.
The foreign ministers of South Africa, Kenya and Tanzania arrived in Kinshasa for talks on ending conflict in the region, foreign ministry officials said.
A spokesman for the opposition in Kinshasa, which has called for negotiations to end the conflict, denounced the loss of civilian lives.

"It's what we feared," Mukendi wa Mulumba, an adviser to the main opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, told Reuters. "The government has opted to sacrifice human lives, particularly the civilian population... We demand the cessation of hostilities."
U.N. envoy Hohammed Sahnoun called for withdrawal of all foreign forces after talks with Zaire officials.

Foreign mercenaries, notably Serbs, are fighting the rebels alongside Zaire's indisciplined army. Zaire accuses neighbouring Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of fighting alongside the rebels. All three deny the charge.
Ogata called for an end to the air raids and a halt to the militarisation by Hutu hardliners of Tingi Tingi camp, 200 km (125 miles) south of Zaire's third city of Kisangani.
"If the camp becomes militarised, it'll become a base for offensives and a target for counter-offensives," she told a Geneva news conference after a trip to the region.
"All those bringing in things to the camp and those involved in military activity must stop this and I hope the international community will support this."
Zaire's ethnic Tutsis took up arms after local authorities tried to expel them to their ancestral homeland in Rwanda.

The war in eastern Zaire is intertwined with the ethnic conflict between Hutus and Tutsis in Rwanda. Hutu hardliners massacred up to 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994 before fleeing en masse into Zaire.
